_comment: What each check verifies and how, in plain words — shown on the board's gate wall.
`checks` is keyed by the check's bracket token ([G01], [E04], [F12]).
`setup` matches the setup (conformance) checks by their title; {x} stands for the
field or tag the title names, and fills the same slot in `key` and the text.
`key` is the check's key in feedback.json, so the card can show what the player was told.
Written from each test's own code. When a test changes, change its entry.

G01.name: Standard opening position
G01.what: A new game starts from the standard backgammon setup, with white to move and the cube in the middle.
G01.how: Calls the engine's opening-position and new-game functions directly: every point must match the standard layout, white must be to move in the roll phase, the cube must be 1 and unowned, the bar and off trays empty, no winner, and each colour's opponent must be the other colour.

G02.name: Pip counts
G02.what: Pip counts — how far each side still has to travel — are right on a new game.
G02.how: Counts pips on the standard opening position with the game's own counting: 167 for each side. The standard opening, not the game's own, so a wrong setup is told once, as the setup.

G03.name: Dice give the right number of moves
G03.what: Doubles give four moves and an ordinary roll gives two.
G03.how: From the opening position, asks how many dice can be used: 3-3-3-3 must allow four, 3-1 two, and black's 6-6-6-6 four. Through the running server: seeds a later turn on the standard board — the opening roll itself is one die per side and can never be four (G31) — rolls until doubles come up, and requires four equal dice with all four still to play, at least one legal move, and at least three of the four dice playable.

G04.name: Blocked points
G04.what: A checker can't land on a point held by two or more opposing checkers.
G04.how: White on 8 with black holding 5 with two checkers: a 3 must give no moves.

G05.name: Play the higher die
G05.what: When only one of the two dice can be played, the player must play the higher one.
G05.how: On screen: white on 13 with black holding 6 three deep, a 3 and a 4 to play, only one usable. The player picks up the piece; a visible hint for the 3 that plays when clicked is told as letting the smaller number play, one that does not as showing it. No hint for the 3 passes.

G06.name: Entering from the bar
G06.what: A checker on the bar must come back in first, and a player who can't enter has no move.
G06.how: White on the bar with a 2 must have exactly one move, entering on 23. With black holding 23 and 21, a roll of 2 and 4 must leave no legal moves.

G07.name: Hitting sends a checker to the bar
G07.what: Landing on a single opposing checker hits it and sends it to the bar.
G07.how: White on 8 moves onto a lone black checker on 5 with a 3: the move must report a hit, white must now sit on 5, black must have one checker on the bar, and point 8 must be empty.

G08.name: Bearing off, including a bigger die
G08.what: Bearing off works, including using a bigger die than needed when no checker is further back.
G08.how: White with two checkers on 3 and the rest off can bear off from 3 with a 5. With checkers on 5 and 3, a 5 must bear off from 5 only — never from 3.

G09.name: No bearing off until all are home
G09.what: No bearing off while any checker is still outside home.
G09.how: White on 3 with another on 8: a 3 must not bear off, and the position must report that not all checkers are home.

G10.name: Single, gammon or backgammon
G10.what: A finished game is classed correctly as a single win, a gammon or a backgammon.
G10.how: White has all 15 off in each case. Black with 2 already off → single. Black with none off, none on the bar and none in white's home → gammon. A black checker in white's home, or on the bar → backgammon. White with only 14 off → not won.

G11.name: Doubling on the player's turn
G11.what: On the player's turn, with the cube centered, the player may offer a double.
G11.how: Through the running server: seeds a later turn — the player to act in the roll phase, cube centered, standard opening board — and requires doubling to be allowed (canDouble true). A fresh game sits in the opening roll, where nobody may double yet (G31).

G26.name: The cube starts centered
G26.what: A new game starts with the cube at one, unowned (centered).
G26.how: Through the running server: a new game must have the cube at value 1 with owner null.

G12.name: The computer's cube decisions
G12.what: The computer accepts, declines and offers the cube at its published win-chance thresholds.
G12.how: Even position (30 pips each): win chance 0.5 and every difficulty accepts. Black hopelessly behind (350 against 2): win chance under 0.24 and hard declines. Hard never offers when white owns the cube, offers or holds on a 30-against-61 position exactly as its thresholds say, easy never offers, and hard holds when far too far ahead.

G13.name: Turn flow
G13.what: A die can't be used twice, turns go white → black → white, and a player with no move passes with a clear message.
G13.how: Through the running server with the roll fixed to 1 and 3: after playing the 3, playing it again must leave the remaining dice unchanged. Playing out white's turn, ending it and advancing the computer must hand the turn back to white. With white on the bar and both entry points blocked, rolling 2 and 4 must end the turn with no legal moves and a message reading exactly 'No moves available'.

G14.name: Legal computer moves, and hard beats easy
G14.what: Every move the computer makes is legal, and hard really is stronger than easy.
G14.how: 200 random positions and rolls at each difficulty: every chosen move is replayed through the engine and must be legal and produce the board the computer claims. Then 25 full games with fixed dice, hard as black against easy as white: hard must win more.

G16.name: Port 8002, and a clear error when taken
G16.what: The server listens on port 8002, and a second copy fails clearly instead of hanging.
G16.how: With the server already running, starts a second copy on the same port: within 6 seconds it must exit with an error, and its output must name 8002 and say the port is in use or already taken.

G17.name: Landing on a single checker
G17.what: A checker can land on a point held by a single opposing checker.
G17.how: White on 8 with a single black on 6: a 2 must give exactly the move 8→6.

G18.name: The opening roll with a 6
G18.what: From the opening position a 6 only moves the checkers that are free to move, and every move stays on the board.
G18.how: From the opening position a 6 may only move checkers from 24, 13 and 8, and every move must stay within the board.

G19.name: No bearing off from the bar
G19.what: No bearing off while a checker is still on the bar.
G19.how: White on 2 with a checker on the bar: a 2 must not bear off, and the position must report that not all checkers are home.

G20.name: An accepted double transfers the cube
G20.what: When a double is accepted, the cube becomes 2 and belongs to whoever took it.
G20.how: Through the running server: the player doubles, the computer accepts, and the cube must become 2 owned by black.

G21.name: No doubling after rolling
G21.what: A double can't be offered once the dice are rolled, and trying anyway changes nothing.
G21.how: Through the running server: after rolling, doubling must be disallowed, and trying anyway must leave the cube unchanged.

G22.name: Win chance rises with the lead
G22.what: The computer's win chance never drops as it gets further ahead.
G22.how: Four positions ordered by growing pip lead — far behind, near even, ahead, and far ahead: the win chance at each must be at least the one before.

G23.name: Undo restores the board
G23.what: Undo returns the board to exactly where it was before the move.
G23.how: Plays a move through the API, calls undo, and asserts points, bar, and off trays deep-equal the pre-move snapshot.

G24.name: Accepting the computer's double
G24.what: Accepting the computer's double makes the cube 2 and owned by the player.
G24.how: Sets a double-offered state, accepts through the response endpoint, and asserts the cube is value 2 owner white in both the response and persisted state.

G25.name: The computer takes its turn
G25.what: After the player ends a turn, the computer takes its turn and control returns to the player.
G25.how: Rolls, completes white's moves, ends the turn, drives the AI turn through the API, and asserts the turn comes back to white.

G27.name: Finished games are counted and carried
G27.what: gamesPlayed counts finished games: it goes up by one when a game ends, and a new game carries it forward.
G27.how: Through the running server: sets one white piece left to bear off, rolls 2-1 and bears it off (the win itself is G08's and G10's), then requires gamesPlayed to have gone up ([aspect: counted]), and after /api/new neither lower ([aspect: carried]) nor higher ([aspect: extra]).

G28.name: The debug route honours turnOver and gamesPlayed
G28.what: The debug state route accepts the turnOver flag and the gamesPlayed count like the other state fields.
G28.how: Through the running server: post turnOver and gamesPlayed to the debug state route and require both to be reflected in the resulting state.

G29.name: Any non-API path serves the game page
G29.what: A path outside /api serves the game page instead of 404ing.
G29.how: Through the running server: fetch a non-/api path and require the HTML page (status 200 with a text/html content type).

G30.name: The computer plays the higher die when only one is playable
G30.what: When only one of the computer's two dice can actually be played, it plays the higher one.
G30.how: Through the engine: on fixed one-move boards, drive the AI's move chooser at every difficulty several times and require every chosen move to be legal (never the lower die).

G31.name: The opening roll decides who goes first
G31.what: A game opens with one die per side: the higher side moves first and plays both numbers, equal dice tie and roll again, and nobody may double before the opening move is played.
G31.how: Through the running server at easy: fixes the opening roll on the debug route, then rolls — 6-5 must give the player the turn ([aspect: won]) in the move phase with a 6 and a 5 to play ([aspect: dice]); 3-5 must give the computer the turn ([aspect: first]), and its AI move must move black exactly 8 pips ([aspect: numbers]) and hand the turn back ([aspect: handback]); 4-4 must stay in phase openingRoll ([aspect: tie]); a fresh game must report canDouble false ([aspect: cube]), and a double asked for anyway (refused or ignored) must leave the cube at 1, no offer pending and no winner ([aspect: cubemoved]).

G32.name: When the computer is stuck, the game says so and the turn returns
G32.what: When the computer is on the bar with every entry point held and rolls numbers it cannot use, its turn ends with the turn handed back to the player and a message containing the words "No moves available".
G32.how: Through the running server: fixes a position where the computer is on the bar and all six entry points are held by two or more opposing pieces, then drives the computer's turn with a 6-5 it cannot use and checks the turn is the player's again ([aspect: pass]) and the message contains the words "No moves available" ([aspect: wording]).

E01.name: Doubles are four moves
E01.what: Doubles really are four moves, not two.
E01.how: From the opening position, 3-3-3-3 must allow four moves and 3-5 two.

E02.name: Bigger die bears off only from the back
E02.what: A bigger-than-needed die only bears off from the highest occupied point.
E02.how: White on 6 and 3 with a 5: bearing off must not be allowed, but 6→1 must be. With only the checker on 3 left, the 5 must bear it off.

E03.name: Exact die always bears off
E03.what: A die that exactly matches a checker's distance always bears it off.
E03.how: White on 6 and 3 with a 3: bearing off from 3 must be allowed.

E04.name: Shut out on the bar
E04.what: A player shut out on the bar has no legal move at all — not even with other checkers.
E04.how: White on the bar, black holding all of 19–24, and white also on 13: with a 3 and a 5, no die may be used and the list of legal moves must be empty.

E05.name: The bar comes first
E05.what: While a checker is on the bar, no other checker may move.
E05.how: White on the bar and on 13 with a 3: there must be moves, and every one must be entering from the bar.

E06.name: Bar counts 25 pips
E06.what: A checker on the bar counts as 25 pips, and borne-off checkers count nothing.
E06.how: One white checker on the bar → 25. Add one on 6 → 31. Add three borne off → still 31. White on the bar and on 4 → 29. Black with two on the bar and one on 20 → 55.

E07.name: On the bar means not all home
E07.what: A checker on the bar means not all checkers are home.
E07.how: White with one checker on 3 is all home; add one on the bar and it must no longer be.

E08.name: Each end position listed once
E08.what: The list of possible turns holds each resulting position once, not once per order of moves.
E08.how: Two white checkers on 10 with a 1 and a 2: there are several orders to play them but only two different end positions, so the list must hold exactly two, all different.

E09.name: Copying a board
E09.what: Copying a board gives a fully independent copy.
E09.how: Copies a board, changes the copy's points, bar and borne-off counts, and checks the original is untouched.

F01.name: The board appears
F01.what: The game page loads and the board appears.
F01.how: Opens the page in a browser and requires the board to be visible.

F02.name: Full board is drawn
F02.what: A new game draws the whole board.
F02.how: Starts a new game and reloads: exactly 24 points and 30 checkers, 15 of each colour.

F03.name: Clicking shows the moves
F03.what: Clicking a checker that can move shows where it can go.
F03.how: Fixes the next roll to 6-5, clicks Roll, clicks a movable checker, and requires at least one move hint to appear.

F04.name: Hints show which die
F04.what: Move hints show which die each move uses.
F04.how: Fixes the roll to 5-3 — the player's die first, so the player wins the opening roll and plays both numbers (a forced 3-5 would hand the turn to the computer) — clicks Roll and the back checker on 13 (another movable checker if it shows nothing): every hint's text must be 3 or 5 (or "off"), and the checker on 13 must show a hint for each die, 3 and 5, both open from it on every board.

F05.name: No-move notice
F05.what: When the player can't move, the page says so.
F05.how: Puts white on the bar with both entry points blocked and fixes the roll to 2-4. After Roll the message must read exactly 'No moves available'.

F06.name: Pip counts on screen
F06.what: The pip counts on screen match the game.
F06.how: On a new game the displayed counts must match the server and the pieces on the board, counted by the grader (a wrong opening is the setup check's complaint, a wrong formula the pip check's). A custom position is then set, and the displayed counts must match the server again.

F07.name: The cube after a double
F07.what: After the player doubles, the cube on screen shows the new value and who owns it.
F07.how: After the player doubles and the computer accepts: value 2, and the owner label names the side the server reports.

F34.name: The cube on a new game
F34.what: A new game shows the cube at one, centered on screen.
F34.how: New game: the cube value reads 1 and the owner label reads centered.

F08.name: Difficulty selector
F08.what: Changing the difficulty and starting a new game really changes it.
F08.how: Selects hard and clicks New game: the server must report hard. Then the same for easy.

F09.name: Hit checker shown on the bar
F09.what: A hit checker is drawn on the bar.
F09.how: Sets a position with one black checker on the bar and reloads: the bar must be visible with exactly one black checker drawn on it.

F10.name: Re-entering shown on the board
F10.what: Coming back in from the bar is shown on the board.
F10.how: White on the bar with the roll fixed to 3-5. After Roll, the entry hints must show on their own, with no click on the bar piece; clicking the bar checker still leaves the two hints showing; clicking one must take the checker off the bar, the server must agree, and a white checker must appear on point 20 or 22.

F11.name: Borne-off checkers in the tray
F11.what: Borne-off checkers appear in the player's off tray.
F11.how: Sets a position with 3 white checkers borne off: the player's tray must be visible with exactly 3 white checkers in it.

F12.name: Win announced
F12.what: A win ends the game with a banner or popup that says the player won.
F12.how: Sets a won position with the message "You win!": the message must show it, and if a modal is open its title must say win (any capitals).

F14.name: Checker animation
F14.how: Reads the page's styles: a checker must have a transition on its position or an animation.

F15.name: Works on either host name
F15.what: The game works whether it's opened at localhost or 127.0.0.1.
F15.how: Loads the page at both addresses: each must show the board with 24 points and 30 checkers and no errors.

F16.name: The player's turn survives a reload
F16.what: Reloading during the player's turn leaves it the player's turn.
F16.how: Reloads a fresh game at the player's turn and requires the reported turn to still be the player's.

F17.name: Match score survives a reload
F17.what: The match score keeps its value across a page reload.
F17.how: Sets the score to 3-5, reloads, and requires the reported score to still be 3 and 5.

F18.name: Dice values survive a reload
F18.what: The rolled dice keep their exact values across a page reload.
F18.how: Sets the dice to 5 and 2, reloads, and requires the reported dice to still be 2 and 5.

F19.name: Difficulty survives a reload
F19.what: The chosen difficulty stays set across a page reload.
F19.how: Sets the difficulty to hard, reloads, and requires it to still be hard.

F20.name: The doubling cube survives a reload
F20.what: Who owns the cube, and therefore whether a double is allowed, stays the same across a reload.
F20.how: Sets the cube to be owned by black, reloads, and requires doubling to still be disallowed for white.

F21.name: Remaining dice survive a reload
F21.what: The dice left to play mid-turn stay the same across a page reload.
F21.how: Sets one die already played (dice 5 and 2, remaining 2), reloads, and requires the remaining die to still be 2.

F22.name: Board resets on new game
F22.what: After a win, clicking New game redraws the standard opening layout and closes the win popup.
F22.how: Sets a won position and clicks New game: exactly 30 checkers, each side back on its opening points, and the modal hidden.

F23.name: New game without reload
F23.what: A new game starts without reloading the page.
F23.how: Sets a won position, marks the window, clicks New game, and then reads the mark: window marks do not survive a page reload, so the mark must still be there.

F24.name: Stuck turn ends
F24.what: When no move can be played, the turn is over and nothing is left to click.
F24.how: Puts white on the bar with both entry points blocked and fixes the roll to 2-4. After Roll the turn must be over with no legal moves, and clicking the bar checker must show no hints.

F25.name: A move uses up a die
F25.what: Playing a move by clicking really advances the turn.
F25.how: Fixes the next roll to 6-5, clicks Roll, clicks a movable checker, clicks one of its visible hints, and requires the move to be played and one fewer die left afterwards.

F26.name: Hint animation
F26.how: Sets white to move with 3-5, clicks a movable checker, and reads the page's styles: the hint it shows must have an animation.

F27.name: Page loads cleanly
F27.what: The game page loads without errors.
F27.how: Opens the page in a browser and requires no console errors and no page errors.

F28.name: Points in board order
F28.what: The 24 points are drawn in the standard board order — the top half runs 13 through 24 left to right, the bottom half 12 down to 1.
F28.how: In a browser: reads the 24 point boxes and requires two rows, one above the other ([aspect: rows] — held back while the tagged points overlap, which is the point-column check's finding), then 13 to 24 along the top and 12 down to 1 along the bottom.

F29.name: Bar between the halves
F29.what: The bar sits between the two board halves, not at the outer edge, and spans both rows.
F29.how: Measures the bar's box and asserts its left edge is right of the left half's right edge, its right edge is left of the right half's left edge, and its height spans both point rows.

F30.name: Triangles point inward
F30.what: Each point's triangle points inward toward the board, not outward.
F30.how: Hides checkers, screenshots the board, samples each point's colour near the outer edge versus the inner end, and asserts the outer edge is triangle paint while the inner end is felt. A point with nothing painted at either end, or painted right across at both ends (a block), has no triangle and is told as such; pointing outward means wider at the inner end than at the rim. Each point is read every 5% of the way in: the painted stretch must narrow away from the rim and stand out from the felt at least half way in, told as all or some of the triangles.

F31.name: Checkers over their own points
F31.what: Every checker is drawn over the point it belongs to, not offset to a neighbour.
F31.how: Measures each checker's centre against its point's centre and vertical band: each sits within a quarter of a point's width of its own point's centre, inside its band. Then each stack must start at the edge of the board: the piece nearest its point's rim within half a piece of it. Judged only once the points are numbered in order (F28): with the numbers wrong, a checker drawn where a player expects it can sit over the wrong number.

F32.name: Off tray visible
F32.what: The off tray is present and visible, not hidden or zero-sized, on the board, at the end where checkers bear off.
F32.how: New game: the off tray exists, is visible, is actually drawn (a fill, an outline or a label — not an empty see-through box), sits over no point, lies on the board (its centre inside the board's frame), lies past points 1 and 24 — the end white and black bear off from (not told while another tray-like element stands at that end: a player can't tell which strip is the tray) — runs at least 90% of the height of the rows of points, and is at least as wide as a checker (at most 90% of a point).

F33.name: A double lets the player make four moves
F33.what: A double gives the player four moves, not two.
F33.how: Sets a doubled dice state through the debug route, reloads, then clicks checker, hint, and move four times, asserting all four dice are consumed; a failure names how many moves the double gave.

F35.name: Board left, controls right
F35.what: The board sits on the left and every button and piece of game info on the right, as the build prompt asks.
F35.how: At 1280×800 and 1440×900 on a new game: the drawn board (points, bar and off tray) starts in the left tenth of the window, and roll, double, undo, end turn, cube, pip counts, turn, message, difficulty and New Game all sit to its right.

F36.name: Board about 80% of the width
F36.what: The board takes about 80% of the window's width, leaving about 20% for the buttons.
F36.how: At both sizes the drawn board must be 70–88% of the window's width (the reference measures 76% and 79%).

F37.name: The game fits the screen
F37.what: Everything fits without scrolling and the board fills the screen's height.
F37.how: At both sizes the page must not scroll either way, a scrollable board must not scroll sideways, no piece may have more than a tenth of its circle past the window's edge, and the drawn board must be at least 70% of the window's height (the reference: 88–89%).

F38.name: Buttons show properly
F38.what: Every button and piece of game info is showing, inside the window, clear of the board and of each other, and big enough to use.
F38.how: At both sizes each control is visible, inside the window and off the board; each button is at least 60×24 px with its label not cut off; no two buttons overlap. A control that isn't showing is named in the line (the Roll button, my pip count, whose turn it is …).

F39.name: Two dice, two moves
F39.what: After any roll exactly two dice are on screen, and two different numbers give exactly two moves (a double's four are F33).
F39.how: Fixes the roll to 6-5 — the player's die first, so the player wins the opening roll and plays both numbers (a forced 5-6 would hand the turn to the computer) — and clicks Roll: two dice on screen, two moves playable by clicking, no third; then seeds a later turn in the move phase with a double already rolled, since an opening roll is one die per side and can no longer be a double (G31): still two dice on screen.

F40.name: Rows line up
F40.what: The top row of points sits straight across from the bottom row, column for column.
F40.how: New game: each row's drawn points sorted left to right; each top point's centre must be within half a point's width of the bottom point in the same column.

F41.name: Checkers are circles sized to their points
F41.what: Every checker is a perfect circle, about 80% as wide as the point it sits on.
F41.how: New game: every checker on a point is drawn round (a circular border radius, clip or SVG circle) with a square box, and the typical checker is 70–90% of a point's width.

F42.name: Points alternate in colour
F42.what: The points alternate between two colours, as on every backgammon board.
F42.how: New game, checkers hidden: each triangle's own colour down its middle at its widest; within each quarter, side-by-side neighbours must differ. Colours are compared with each other only; neither across the bar nor straight across the board is judged, and a point the bar or tray is drawn over is skipped.

F43.name: Every drawn piece shows
F43.what: Every drawn piece on the board can be seen whole: a stack of up to six shows each of its pieces, and no drawn piece is cut off.
F43.how: New game: a grid of spots inside each drawn checker on a point is hit-tested (the pieces made hit-testable for the reading). Two pieces on the same point with centres closer than a third of a piece are drawn on one spot; a piece showing less than three quarters of itself on screen, not because another piece is drawn over it, is cut off. Pieces mostly past the window are the fit check's.

F44.name: Buttons carry their names
F44.what: Each button's label carries its name: Roll, Double, Undo, End Turn and New Game.
F44.how: New game: each button's own text, whether or not it shows, must contain its name (case aside; "Roll Dice" carries Roll). A button that isn't there is the tag check's; one that doesn't show is F38's.

F45.name: Clicking a destination moves there
F45.what: Clicking the point a picked-up checker can move to plays that move.
F45.how: Fixes the roll to 2-1, clicks Roll and the top checker on 13 (its one move is to the empty 11), then clicks three spots up the column of point 11 — near its middle-ward end, its centre, and its edge-ward end, away from the hint token — and requires a checker on 11 each time. A game whose hints play no move is F25's.

F46.name: The decline pop-up says you won
F46.what: When the computer turns down the player's double, the pop-up title contains the word win.
F46.how: Sets a position where the player is far ahead, clicks the double button, and requires the pop-up title to contain win.

F47.name: The turn waits for End Turn
F47.what: The player's turn never ends by itself; it waits for the End Turn click, and Undo keeps working until then.
F47.how: Sets a position white can move in, forces 6-5, plays every die by clicking until the turn is over, then waits 1.6 s: the turn must still be white's in the move phase. Undo must be available and give a die back ([aspect: undo]); after replaying, End Turn must hand the turn to the computer ([aspect: endturn]).

F48.name: A no-move roll passes by itself
F48.what: A roll with no possible move shows the dice and 'No moves available' for about a second, then passes to the computer on its own.
F48.how: Blocks both of white's numbers with nothing on the bar, forces 6-5 and clicks Roll: the dice and a notice saying "No moves available" must be up for a second with the turn still white's ([aspect: notice]), and then the turn must pass to the computer without End Turn.

F49.name: Plain double offer
F49.what: When the computer offers a double the message says so in plain words, not its win percentage, pip counts, or reasoning.
F49.how: A race the hard computer doubles in: after End Turn, something on screen — the message area or any pop-up — must say it is doubling ([aspect: shown]), and that text must not show win chances, pip counts or reasoning; then requires buttons reading Accept (or Take) and Decline (or Pass) to answer it ([aspect: answer]).

F50.name: Plain double answer
F50.what: When the computer answers the player's double it says accept or decline in plain words, not its win percentage or pip counts.
F50.how: The player doubles from an even position (the medium computer takes) and from a hopeless one (it passes): each time something on screen must say what it did ([aspect: shown]), without win chances, pip counts or reasoning.

F51.name: End pop-up names the winner and points
F51.what: The end-of-game pop-up says who won and the points the game was worth, with no 'Match score' line.
F51.how: Ends the game with the player's own last bear-off (F53's move). The end-of-game pop-up must say what the game was worth ([aspect: points]) and must not show a match score.

F52.name: Greyed-out buttons look different
F52.what: Buttons the player can't use look clearly different from usable ones — dimmed and greyed out.
F52.how: New game: Undo and End Turn cannot be used yet, New Game and Roll can. From each button's screenshot, the spread between its brightest and darkest marks; the unusable pair must be at most 60% of the least clear usable button; Roll counts as usable only when it can be clicked (a Roll shut at the start is F61's fault).

F53.name: Bearing off the last piece opens the win pop-up
F53.what: When the player bears off their last piece, the end-of-game pop-up opens at once with a title that says they won.
F53.how: On screen: seed a one-checker bear-off position, play the last checker off, and require the win pop-up to appear immediately.

F54.name: The difficulty control shows the level you're playing
F54.what: After the page reloads, the difficulty control shows the difficulty the game is actually running at, not a fixed default.
F54.how: In a browser: chooses Hard on the difficulty control and clicks New Game (the game really is Hard: F08's), reloads, and requires the control to read hard.

F55.name: The computer finishes its turn after a reload
F55.what: If the player reloads during the computer's turn, the computer finishes that turn and control returns to the player.
F55.how: On screen: seed a position where it is the computer's turn, reload the page, and require the turn to become the player's as the computer completes its turn.

F56.name: The pending double offer shows again after a reload
F56.what: If the player reloads while the computer's double offer is on screen, the offer shows again so the player can accept or decline.
F56.how: Seeds the computer's pending double offer and reloads: visible buttons to take and to pass the double must be on screen again, wherever the page puts them.

F57.name: A tall stack caps at six with a count
F57.what: A point holds at most six drawn checkers; from seven up it draws six and the top piece shows the total.
F57.how: Seven white on 13, drawn at rest: at most six shown on screen ([aspect: cap]), and the total 7 readable on the stack — a checkerCount badge or a number shown on point 13's column ([aspect: count]).

F58.name: The top piece slides away
F58.what: When a checker leaves a stack, the piece farthest from the board's edge is the one that slides away, and the rest stay put.
F58.how: Opening position, 2-1: the pieces on 13 are held in the page, the top one is picked up and played to 11. When a held piece is the one now on 11 it must be the top one; a page that draws every piece afresh leaves none to follow and is not judged.

F59.name: A piece lands at the far end
F59.what: When a checker lands on a point that already holds checkers, it joins at the far end of the stack, farthest from the edge.
F59.how: White to move with a 2 left, one piece on 13 and one on 11: both are held in the page, and the piece on 13 is played onto 11. When both held pieces are the ones on 11, the arrival must be farther from the edge; a page that draws them afresh is not judged.

F60.name: Clicking a piece's column picks it up
F60.what: Clicking anywhere in the column of a point holding one of the player's movable pieces picks up its top piece and shows its hints.
F60.how: Fixes the roll to 2-1, clicks Roll, then clicks a spot in the column of point 13 away from the checker — near the column's middle-ward end — and requires a hint to appear.

F61.name: The opening roll on screen
F61.what: On the opening roll the page shows both dice; equal dice tie and say to roll again; and when the computer's die is higher it makes the first move and hands the turn back.
F61.how: In a browser: first requires the Roll button to be clickable at the start of a new game ([aspect: roll]); then fixes the opening roll to 6-5, clicks Roll, and requires at least two dice on screen once they rest ([aspect: dice]); fixes 4-4 and requires the words "Tie — roll again" (any dash) somewhere on the page, again with two dice resting on screen ([aspect: tie], [aspect: dice]); fixes 3-5 and requires the state to show the computer's pieces moved and the turn back with the player ([aspect: computer]). The player's own first move with both numbers is F03's and F04's, which open with a roll the player wins.

F62.name: The computer's turn pacing on screen
F62.what: When the computer takes its turn, its dice stay readable for about a second before its first piece moves, then each further move follows about half a second after the last.
F62.how: In a browser: sets the opening position with the player's roll used up, easy difficulty and the computer's roll fixed to 6-5, records every frame (the visible dice drawn, the black pieces' centres relative to the board, and their data-loc tags), and clicks End Turn. Requires End Turn available and the state to show the computer moved and the turn back ([aspect: turn]); the black pieces to move on screen ([aspect: drawn]); a new dice drawing before the first move ([aspect: dice]) that stayed unchanged at least 0.8 s ([aspect: first]); and at least two move starts, each at least 0.35 s after the last ([aspect: between]); moves are timed from the pieces' tags, or from their drawing when the tags show fewer than two moves.

F63.name: The opening dice carry whose they are
F63.what: After the opening roll the state carries the dice as [playerDie, computerDie], and each die on screen is marked data-owner "you" or "ai".
F63.how: In a browser: fixes the opening roll to 6-5, clicks Roll, and requires the state's dice to read [6,5] ([aspect: order]) and the visible dice to include one marked data-owner "you" and one marked "ai" ([aspect: owner]).

F64.name: The Fast Forward button appears only in a race
F64.what: On your turn in a pure race — nothing on the bar and every one of your checkers past every one of the computer's — a button appears to play the rest out for you; anywhere else, like the opening position, it stays hidden.
F64.how: In a browser: on a new game requires the fastForwardBtn button hidden ([aspect: outside]); then sets a race on the player's turn (every piece home on both sides) and requires the button visible with a label containing "Fast Forward" ([aspect: shown]).

F65.name: Fast Forward plays a race out to the end
F65.what: Clicking Fast Forward plays the rest of the game out for both sides without any further clicks, and when it ends the end-of-game pop-up shows who won.
F65.how: In a browser: sets a short race (white one piece on each of 1-3, black one on each of 22-24, the rest borne off), fixes the rolls to 2-1, 2-1, 6-5 so the play-out takes three turns including the computer's, records every frame (the dice drawn and the white pieces), and clicks Fast Forward once. Requires the game to reach gameover within a minute ([aspect: played]) and the end-of-game pop-up ([aspect: popup]); and, for the player's first turn, a new dice drawing before the first move ([aspect: dice]) up at least 0.8 s ([aspect: first]) and the moves at least 0.35 s apart ([aspect: between]), timed as F62 times the computer.

F66.name: Fast Forward can be paused and carried on
F66.what: While Fast Forward is running the button reads "Pause"; clicking Pause stops the play-out and the button reads "Fast Forward" again; clicking it then carries on.
F66.how: In a browser: sets a long race (fifteen a side, all home), clicks Fast Forward and requires the button to read Pause ([aspect: running]); clicks it 250 ms later and requires it to read Fast Forward again ([aspect: label]) and the position unchanged from 2 s to 5 s after ([aspect: paused]); clicks it again and requires Pause ([aspect: running]) and a changed position within 15 s ([aspect: resume]).

F67.name: A computer double stops Fast Forward until you answer
F67.what: If the computer offers a double while Fast Forward is running, the play-out stops and stays stopped; after you answer the double it still stays stopped until you click Fast Forward again.
F67.how: In a browser: sets F49's position (hard, the player's moves done, a race the computer doubles in by the published thresholds) and clicks Fast Forward. Requires the offer on screen wherever the page shows it ([aspect: offer]), the button not reading Pause 1.5 s later ([aspect: stopped]), a button to take the double ([aspect: answer]); after taking it, the turn back with the player ([aspect: back]), the position unchanged from 2 s to 5 s after ([aspect: stays]), and the button showing and reading Fast Forward ([aspect: back]).

F68.name: On load the difficulty control reads the game's level
F68.what: When the page opens, the difficulty control shows the difficulty the game is actually running at, whatever set it.
F68.how: In a browser: starts a new game at Hard through /api/new, reloads, and requires the difficulty control to read hard (the player's own choice is F54's).

F69.name: The pip elements hold just the number
F69.what: pipWhite and pipBlack contain only the pip count, with any label outside those elements.
F69.how: In a browser: opens a new game and requires the text of pipWhite and pipBlack to be a bare number (F06 judges the numbers themselves).

F70.name: Triangles leave a gap across the middle
F70.what: The tip of each top-half triangle and the tip of the bottom-half triangle directly across the middle leave a clear gap — about 24% of the board's half-height — neither touching nor crossing, and not so short that the gap is wider than that.
F70.how: Measures each point's painted tip from a screenshot, pairs top and bottom points by column, and checks the gap as a fraction of the point's height against the 19%–29% band (≤0 touching, <19% too close, >29% too wide).

F71.name: Checkers on a point stack evenly, tighter at six
F71.what: The checkers on a point stack evenly apart (two to five pieces), and a full stack of six sits a little tighter.
F71.how: Reads checker boxes by data-loc, sorts by centre y, and compares consecutive pitch: even within a stack for two to five pieces, and a six-piece stack's pitch at least ~3% tighter than the even pitch. Also measures each stack's extent — the mean pitch against the median checker width — flagging stacks that reach too far (spread) or crowd at the edge (bunched), and requiring a six-stack to compress. Also checks horizontal alignment — a stack's pieces share one x, and a stack whose centres fan out more than a tenth of a checker width drifts sideways (cascades) instead of standing in a single straight column over its point.

setup.name: Server starts
setup.what: The server starts and serves the game.
setup.how: Runs the server with its start command and waits for it to answer on port 8002.

setup.name: Health check answers
setup.what: The health address answers.

setup.name: Health check returns data

setup.title: the health body carries status "ok"
setup.name: Health check says ok

setup.how: Sets a position through the debug route and checks the reply's points field is an array of 26 numbers.

setup.name: Setting a position

setup.how: Sets a known position and requires the request to come back without an error.

setup.title: a queued dice roll is honoured
setup.name: Fixing the next roll
setup.what: A roll queued through the debug route is the next roll.
setup.how: Queues 6-1, rolls, and requires the dice to come back as 1 and 6.

setup.title: the debug roll endpoint answers without error
setup.name: The roll route answers
setup.what: A roll queued through the debug route comes back without an error.
setup.how: Queues 6-1, rolls, and requires the request to come back without an error.

setup.what: The page has the "{x}" element that automation looks for.
setup.how: Loads the page and looks for an element tagged data-testid="{x}".

setup.title: the page keeps the id "{x}"
setup.name: Page id "{x}"
setup.what: The page's "{x}" element keeps its id "{x}" as well as its tag, as the build prompt requires of every static element.
setup.how: Loads the page and looks for an element with id="{x}".

setup.title: 24 board points are drawn
setup.name: 24 points drawn

setup.how: Loads a new game and counts the drawn points: exactly 24.

setup.title: 24 board points are tagged for automation
setup.name: 24 points tagged
setup.what: All 24 points carry the tag automation uses.
setup.how: Counts elements tagged as points: exactly 24.

setup.title: each point's tag is on its own column
setup.name: Each point its own column
setup.what: Each point's tag sits on that point's column — the upright rectangle its triangle stands in, from the board's edge to the middle — so no two tagged points overlap, as the build prompt requires.
setup.how: Loads the page, reads the box of every element tagged as a point, and requires no two to overlap by more than a sliver (4 px each way).

setup.name: 30 checkers drawn
setup.what: The board draws all 30 checkers.

setup.what: All 30 checkers carry the tag automation uses.

stages_note: Player order. The model hears only the failing checks of the earliest stage that has any: a player cannot reach a later stage past an earlier one that is broken. Every check is still graded every round. A key ending in / matches every setup check under it; the most specific key wins.
